Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN)  -- The operator of a trolley that rear-ended another trolley should have been able to see the other vehicle was stopped 480 feet ahead, a federal investigator said Monday. Passengers walk past firefighters at a Green Line station in Boston after the trolley collision Friday evening. The trolley driver has told investigators he was text messaging during Friday night's collision, which injured 20 people. The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority, which previously had banned operators from using cell phones and other portable devices, now has told employees to leave the devices at home while on duty, National Transportation Safety Board member Debbie Hersman said Monday. Hersman also noted investigators have determined that the operator may have missed some crucial indications of a stopped trolley ahead on the tracks.  Watch new transit rule on cell phones » . "There were several signals -- two green signals, a yellow signal and a red signal -- coming out of the station, and the point of collision occurred 80 feet past that red signal," Hersman said. "We did a site-distance test, and we know that the operator had the ability to see the trolley stopped in front of him 480 feet in advance of the collision." Boston officials said over the weekend that the trolley operator was using his cell phone. Numerous media outlets, including CNN's Boston affiliates, have identified the driver as 24-year-old Aiden Quinn. "The operator of the striking train was interviewed at the hospital by two detectives," said MBTA general manager Daniel Grabauskas. "He admitted that he was texting at the time of the accident." The operator told detectives that, when he looked up, "it was too late as he applied the brake and the train struck the other trolley," Grabauskas said. He described himself as "outraged." "We have reinforced for a number of years that the use of cell phones or any other kinds of electronic devices while operating a train or a bus is absolutely prohibited," Grabauskas said. Though the investigation is ongoing, he said, the two-year employee will be fired if his version of events is confirmed. None of the injuries was considered life-threatening, the MBTA said. The collision happened at 7:18 p.m. ET Friday as the Green Line trains were traveling between the Park Street and Government Center stations in downtown Boston. Both trains were traveling westbound when one train rear-ended the second, an MBTA official said. A train operator also was text messaging last year in a California train crash that killed 25 people. CNN's Rob Frehse and Gary Bender contributed to this report.

**BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN)** — A federal investigator said Monday that the trolley operator who struck another trolley from behind had a clear opportunity to see the stopped vehicle from 480 feet away.

After Friday evening’s Green Line collision in Boston, passengers walked past firefighters at the station. Twenty people were injured in the crash.

The operator told investigators that he had been sending text messages when the collision occurred Friday night. According to National Transportation Safety Board member Debbie Hersman, the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority had already prohibited train and bus operators from using cell phones and other portable electronics. The agency has now instructed on-duty employees to leave such devices at home.

Hersman said investigators also believe the operator may have failed to notice several important warnings that another trolley was stopped on the tracks.

She explained that the route leaving the station included two green signals, followed by a yellow light and then a red one. The crash occurred 80 feet beyond the red signal. A visibility test conducted at the location showed that the driver could have seen the trolley ahead from 480 feet before impact.

Boston authorities said during the weekend that the operator had been using his phone. Several news organizations, including CNN’s Boston affiliates, identified him as 24-year-old Aiden Quinn.

MBTA General Manager Daniel Grabauskas said two detectives questioned the operator at the hospital, where he acknowledged that he was texting when the accident happened. According to Grabauskas, the driver said that by the time he looked up, there was not enough time to stop; he applied the brake, but the train still hit the trolley ahead.

Grabauskas said he was “outraged.” He emphasized that for years the MBTA has made clear that operators are strictly forbidden from using cell phones or any other electronic devices while driving a train or bus.

Although the inquiry remains underway, Grabauskas said the operator, who had worked for the agency for two years, would be dismissed if his account was verified.

The MBTA reported that none of the 20 injuries was life-threatening.

The collision took place at 7:18 p.m. Eastern Time on Friday, while two Green Line trains were moving between the Park Street and Government Center stations in downtown Boston. An MBTA official said both were heading west when the trailing train crashed into the rear of the other.

A train operator was also texting during a California rail accident the previous year that left 25 people dead.

CNN’s Rob Frehse and Gary Bender contributed to the report.

### Texting Driver Rear-Ends Boston Trolley, Injuring 20

**BOSTON** — Twenty people were injured when a Green Line trolley operator who was texting rear-ended another trolley, authorities said.

The collision occurred after the operator failed to stop before striking a trolley ahead on the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority line. Emergency crews treated passengers and transported some to area hospitals. The injuries were not believed to be life-threatening.

Transit officials said the driver admitted using a cellphone at the time of the crash. The operator was removed from service as investigators examined the circumstances surrounding the collision.

The incident prompted renewed scrutiny of cellphone use by public transit employees. Officials said operators are prohibited from texting or using personal electronic devices while driving.

Service was disrupted while crews cleared the damaged trolleys and inspected the tracks. The MBTA said it was cooperating with the investigation and reviewing its safety procedures.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the NTSB’s findings on the 2009 Boston trolley collision, including the signals, stopping distance, cell phone policy, injuries, and statements from MBTA officials.
counterfactuals.output:
The NTSB concluded that the May 8, 2009, MBTA Green Line rear-end collision near Government Center was caused by the striking trolley operator’s distraction while text-messaging.

- **Signals:** The signal system was functioning properly. The operator passed restrictive wayside signals—including a red stop signal—without responding appropriately. Event-recorder evidence showed no meaningful braking until only seconds before impact.
- **Stopping distance:** Investigators determined that the stopped trolley was visible far enough ahead for the following trolley to stop. Braking tests indicated it could have stopped within roughly 150–200 feet, less than the available sight distance, had the operator reacted promptly.
- **Cell phone use and policy:** Phone records showed the operator had been exchanging numerous text messages, with a message sent shortly before the crash. At the time, MBTA rules prohibited employees from using personal electronic devices while operating, but did not prohibit carrying them, and the NTSB found enforcement inadequate. It cited that weak enforcement as a contributing factor. The MBTA subsequently adopted a stricter zero-tolerance policy barring operators from possessing cell phones or similar devices while on duty.
- **Injuries:** There were no fatalities. The striking operator was seriously injured, and 49 passengers suffered mostly minor injuries and were taken to hospitals.
- **MBTA officials’ statements:** MBTA officials said the signal system had worked as intended and characterized the crash as operator error. Then-general manager Daniel Grabauskas said the operator had admitted texting, moved to dismiss him, and announced tougher restrictions on employees carrying electronic devices. The NTSB agreed that texting was the immediate cause but emphasized that MBTA management also bore responsibility for failing to enforce its existing rule effectively.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

**Monday, May 11, 2009 — Breaking News**

### Green Line operator was texting before Friday crash, investigators say

**BOSTON** — The operator of a Green Line trolley that rear-ended another train Friday night told federal investigators he had been using his cell phone moments before the collision, officials said Monday.

Aiden Quinn, 24, acknowledged that he was texting his girlfriend and failed to notice a red signal before his trolley struck a stopped train in the tunnel near Government Center. Dozens of passengers were injured in the accident, along with Quinn and another MBTA employee.

“He stated he was texting his girlfriend at the time of the accident,” National Transportation Safety Board official Debbie Hersman said while discussing the agency’s preliminary investigation. Investigators were examining train data, signals and other evidence to determine the trolley’s speed and whether Quinn attempted to brake.

MBTA General Manager Daniel Grabauskas called the conduct unacceptable and said Quinn would be dismissed if the investigation confirmed his admission. “This is a clear violation of our rules,” Grabauskas said.

Grabauskas also announced a tougher policy barring operators from carrying cell phones and other personal electronic devices while on duty. Employees found using such devices while operating MBTA equipment could face immediate termination.

The crash disrupted Green Line service Friday evening and renewed concerns about distracted driving on public-transit systems. Federal investigators said their inquiry was continuing and that Monday’s findings were preliminary.

counterfactuals.output:
**Texting trolley driver blamed for Boston subway crash that injured dozens**

**BOSTON —** A Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority trolley operator was sending text messages moments before his Green Line train slammed into the back of a stopped trolley in a Boston subway tunnel, injuring nearly 50 people, federal investigators found.

The May 8, 2009, collision occurred between Government Center and Park Street stations during the evening rush hour. Investigators said the operator, 24-year-old Aiden Quinn, failed to obey a red signal and did not react in time to the trolley stopped ahead of him.

The National Transportation Safety Board concluded that the stationary trolley was visible from about **480 feet away**, giving Quinn sufficient distance to recognize the danger and stop had he been paying attention.

Instead, investigators said, Quinn was exchanging text messages with his girlfriend as his two-car train continued through the tunnel. He applied the brakes only moments before impact, and the moving trolley struck the rear of the stopped train at significant speed.

Dozens of passengers were taken to hospitals, though no one was killed. Quinn was among those seriously injured. The crash also caused extensive damage to both trains and disrupted service on one of Boston’s busiest subway lines.

Quinn initially told investigators he may have blacked out before the crash. Evidence gathered from his cellphone, however, showed that he had been texting immediately beforehand. Authorities said distraction—not a medical emergency or mechanical failure—was the central cause.

The NTSB determined the probable cause was Quinn’s failure to comply with the signal because he was distracted by his cellphone. Investigators also identified broader safety concerns, including the absence of an automatic train-control system capable of stopping a trolley that passed a red signal.

The MBTA fired Quinn and adopted a strict policy barring trolley, subway and bus operators from carrying cellphones or other personal electronic devices while on duty. The agency also increased enforcement and warned that employees who violated the rule could be dismissed.

Quinn later faced criminal charges and pleaded guilty to negligence-related offenses. The case became a prominent example of the dangers of texting while operating public transportation and prompted transit agencies around the country to review their own rules governing electronic devices.
